implementation_notes: Python ships the pattern as a standard-library primitive: functools.partial(func, *args, **keywords) "freezes" some arguments and returns a callable with a simplified signature, exposing .args and .keywords so wrappers and frameworks can inspect what was bound, and functools.partialmethod provides the descriptor form for methods. Closures can do the same job, but a partial preserves the binding as data instead of hiding it in a lambda, which is why libraries (logging, multiprocessing, click) special-case partial objects. Python's idiomatic substitute at call sites is default and keyword arguments; reach for partial when the specialised function itself has to travel.
code_sketch:
from functools import partial

def power(base, exponent):
    return base ** exponent

square = partial(power, exponent=2)      # keyword binding
square(5)                                 # 25, base supplied later
parse_de = partial(parse, locale='de-DE')
pitfalls: partial appends call-time positional arguments after the frozen ones, so only leading parameters can be bound positionally; a non-leading argument needs a keyword binding or an explicit lambda.
A partial has no __name__ of its own and a partial of a bound method keeps a strong reference to the instance - use functools.update_wrapper and mind the lifetime.
Call-time keywords override the ones stored on the partial, so the binding can be silently defeated, and re-creating the partial per call allocates.

variants.name: Closure / lambda that captures the bound value
variants.implementation_notes: A lambda or a small named function closes over the bound value and produces the reduced-arity callable with no library involvement; it is the shortest form inside comprehensions and callbacks and the only one that can reorder arguments or add logic while binding. It gives up what partial offers - .args/.keywords for introspection, framework special-casing, and a signature that tools can read - so prefer partial when the specialised value must be inspected or handed to a framework, and a named def when the specialisation deserves a docstring and a stable name in tracebacks.
pitfalls: A lambda has no name, so tracebacks, profilers and logs point at <lambda>; name the specialisation with def when it is part of an API.
Late binding: a lambda created in a loop over a variable captures the variable, so every specialisation sees the final value (bind it with a default argument: lambda y, x=x: ...).
